units.title: Memory System Architecture: Idea Unit Segmentation Repair and Dual-Labeling Strategy
units.summary: The memory system's transcript processing involves idea unit extraction and segmentation, with ongoing discussions on granularity, quality, and a dual-labeling strategy. A repair mechanism has been adopted for idea unit segmentation to handle incomplete fragments by merging fragmented sentences with their most relevant context, ensuring information completeness and preventing omissions. To optimize retrieval, the system will adopt a dual-labeling strategy where memory items will have two types of labels: one for content/theme and another for its type (e.g., 'to-do'), allowing users to search by both. This strategy addresses the key open issue of the memory retrieval strategy, specifically how to prioritize searching by theme/segment tags or functional tags (like to-do), and if both types of tags should be retained and how the retrieval process should be designed. For idea unit labeling, the system aims for a single precise label, allowing multiple initial candidates but enforcing a final limit of two. Text segmentation performance evaluation requires a benchmark dataset with pre-labeled breakpoints.

units.title: Memory System Architecture: Hierarchical Structure, Time-based vs. Topic-based Models, Parallel Processing, Duplicate Candidate Management, and Human-in-the-loop Importance Tuning
units.summary: The long-term memory (LTM) system features a three-tier hierarchical structure: L1 nodes representing fine-grained idea units from a single meeting, L2 nodes summarizing a block of L1s (e.g., from four meetings), and L3 nodes providing the highest-level summary. This hierarchical data structure organizes conversation content. Architectural debates exist between time-based and topic-based LTM models, impacting how revisited topics are handled. The time-based model proposes creating new L1 nodes for each topic mention based on meeting chronology, and for retrieval in such a time-oriented structure, L1 units should be provided along with their L2/L3 parent nodes to give LLMs necessary temporal context. The topic-based model suggests organizing nodes by semantic themes and updating existing L1 nodes with new information and timestamps to maintain an evolutionary history. Key node attributes include 'Importance', 'Relevance', and 'Recency'/'Activation'. To preserve the historical significance of an idea, its static 'importance' score should be separated from the dynamic 'activation' parameter that handles decay, preventing important but old ideas from disappearing entirely due to time, as 'activation' decreases but high importance items can have a baseline. A human-in-the-loop system for tuning memory node 'importance' is planned, where the system will use similarity search to suggest related idea units for adjustment. The design of this human-in-the-loop system remains an open issue, specifically regarding how users will inspect and adjust scores and how the system can proactively suggest related units for tuning. Memory node updates and merges are limited to within a single meeting, and parallel processing of idea units by multiple agents requires duplicate candidate management.

units.title: System Demonstration Strategy: Dynamic Visualization
units.summary: The strategy for demonstrating the memory system involves a dynamic visualization of the evolving memory graph as it processes meetings, showcasing human-in-the-loop inspection and tuning capabilities. A dynamic visualization tool will be created to animate the construction and updating of the memory graph over time, making abstract concepts like node creation, updates, and decay tangible for development and presentation purposes. A new guideline for prompt engineering was also adopted, requiring prompts and presentation materials (like a slide deck of important prompts) to be made more generic and avoid internal project jargon (e.g., 'L1 agent') to improve language model comprehension and system generalizability.
